\mxunit{enrichment-telescoping-solutions}{Telescoping sums}
\mxsubtitle{High school · sequences \textperiodcentered{} Worked solutions \textperiodcentered{} 10}

\begin{exercise}
Find $\sum [\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k+1}]$ from $k=3$ to 10.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
Interior terms cancel: $\frac{1}{3}-\frac{1}{11}=\frac{8}{33}$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Express $\frac{1}{k(k+2)}$ as a difference of two fractions.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$\frac{1}{k(k+2)}=(\frac{1}{2})[\frac{1}{k}-\frac{1}{k+2}]$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
Find $\sum (2k+1)$ from $k=0$ to n using $(k+1)^{2}-k^{2}$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$2k+1=(k+1)^{2}-k^{2}$. The sum is $(n+1)^{2}-0^{2}=(n+1)^{2}$.
\end{solution}

\begin{exercise}
If $S_{n}=\frac{n}{n+1}$, find the least integer $n\geq 1$ with $1-S_{n}<\num{0,01}$.
\end{exercise}
\begin{solution}
$\frac{1}{n+1}<\frac{1}{100}$ means $n+1>100$, hence $n\geq 100$. The minimum is 100.
\end{solution}

\begin{problem}[Investigate, justify, conclude]
Let $T_{n}=\sum  \frac{1}{k(k+2)}$ for k from 1 to n. Derive an exact formula and find its limit. Find the least n such that the gap to the limit is strictly less than $\num{0,01}$.
\end{problem}
\begin{solution}
After decomposition, all except the first two and last two terms cancel: $T_{n}=\frac{3}{4}-\frac{1}{2(n+1)}-\frac{1}{2(n+2)}$. The limit is $\frac{3}{4}$. The gap decreases with n. At $n=98$ it is $\frac{1}{198}+\frac{1}{200}>\num{0,01}$; at $n=99$ it is $\frac{1}{200}+\frac{1}{202}<\num{0,01}$. Therefore the minimum is 99.
\end{solution}
